pair.title: Only the part of the spin square to your floor turns a pendulum
pair.mini: A Foucault pendulum's swing plane turns at the rate of the Earth's spin that stands square to the floor. On a globe that is zero at the equator and reversed south of it. On a spinning disc it would be the same everywhere.
pair.text: A pendulum's swing plane turns only by the part of the Earth's rotation that stands square to the local floor. On a globe that part is Ω sin φ: all of it at the poles, none at the equator, and reversed south of it, so pendulums in the southern hemisphere turn the other way. On a spinning flat disc, every floor is square to the axis, so every pendulum would turn at the full rate, the same way, everywhere. The flat model as usually held has no daily spin at all and predicts no turning anywhere; the disc is lent one here to give it its best chance. The pendulum at the South Pole in 2001 turned the opposite way from every northern one [1].
pair.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: Foucault pendulums turning the same way and at the same rate at every latitude, or not turning at all.
axis.title: The spin axis and your floor
axis.mini: At any place on a globe, the Earth's spin axis rises above the horizon at an angle equal to the latitude: that is why the celestial pole stands at your latitude, and why a pendulum turns at Ω sin φ.
axis.text: One station on the globe. The Earth's spin axis passes through the centre; seen from the station it rises above the horizontal at an angle equal to the latitude φ, which is why the celestial pole stands at an altitude equal to your latitude. That angle decides how much of the rotation a floor feels: the part square to the floor is Ω sin φ. At the poles the axis is vertical and the floor turns at the full rate; at the equator it lies flat and the floor does not turn at all. The drawing is schematic.
axis.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: a pendulum's turning rate that does not follow the latitude.
anim.title: What a pendulum on a turning floor does
anim.labels: Floor held still|Swing plane held still
anim.mini: The same motion drawn in two frames: the floor's, where the swing plane creeps round, and the swing's, where the floor turns beneath it. At latitude 0° both go still, because sin 0 = 0. The latitude is named above.
anim.text: A Foucault pendulum seen from straight above, at the latitude named above the text. In the frame of the floor, the swing plane creeps round; in the frame of the swing, the floor turns beneath it. Nothing about the pendulum changes between the two, only what is held fixed on the screen. The rate is the Earth's rotation times sin φ [2]: set the latitude to 0° and both pictures go still. At the pole the swing frame is the frame of the stars; elsewhere it is the frame in which the plane is carried along the surface. Foucault first showed it in Paris in 1851 [1]. Swing rate and time are both scaled, with the factors printed on the image; the angle swept is real.
anim.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: pendulums at every latitude turning at the same rate, or not at all.
split.title: Where the sine comes from
split.mini: At one place, the Earth's rotation vector splits into a part along the local vertical and a part along the floor. Only the vertical part, Ω sin φ, turns a pendulum's swing plane.
split.text: At one station, the Earth's rotation vector Ω can be split into two parts: one along the local vertical, of size Ω sin φ, and one lying along the floor, Ω cos φ. A pendulum swinging freely feels only the vertical part as a turning of its swing plane; the horizontal part only tilts it imperceptibly [1]. So the precession rate is Ω sin φ: 15.04° per hour at the poles, 11.3° per hour at Paris, zero at the equator, and negative, meaning the other way round, in the southern hemisphere. The drawing is schematic.
split.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: precession rates that do not scale with the sine of the latitude.
omega.title: One rotation vector, three floors
omega.mini: The Earth's rotation is one arrow, the same everywhere, parallel to the axis. What changes is your floor. Near the pole the arrow stands up out of it; near the equator it lies flat in it. The upright part, Ω sin φ, is the whole of the precession.
omega.text: Ω is the same arrow everywhere: same direction, same length, parallel to the Earth's axis. What changes from place to place is the floor. Near the pole the arrow stands almost straight up out of the floor, and nearly all of it counts; near the equator it lies almost flat in the floor, and almost none of it does. The vertical piece, drawn in teal, is Ω sin φ, and it is the whole of the pendulum's precession rate [1]. On a disc spinning about a vertical axis, every floor would see the whole arrow, the same way up.
omega.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: the same precession rate at every latitude, as a disc spinning about a vertical would give.
rose.title: What you actually watch in Paris
rose.mini: A pendulum's track over six hours at the latitude of Paris, seen on the floor. The swing plane creeps round at 11.3° per hour, so the star pattern closes after about 32 hours.
rose.text: What you actually watch: the bob's track over six hours at the latitude of Paris, drawn in the frame of the floor. The swing plane creeps round at 11.3° per hour, 15.04° times sin 48.85°, so the star pattern closes up after about 32 hours, not 24. Foucault showed it in the Panthéon in 1851 with a 67 m wire and a 28 kg bob [1]. The narrow ellipse of each swing is exaggerated here so successive swings can be told apart; in a real pendulum it is what the experimenter works hardest to make smaller.
rose.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: a swing plane in Paris that does not turn, or turns once in 24 hours.
lat.title: Three models, three curves
lat.mini: Precession rate against latitude. The globe's sine crosses zero at the equator and changes sign. A spinning disc gives one rate everywhere; a still flat Earth gives none. The South Pole pendulum of 2001 turned the other way.
lat.text: Precession rate against latitude for three models. The globe's curve, Ω sin φ, crosses zero at the equator and changes sign south of it. A spinning disc is a horizontal line at the full rotation rate. A stationary flat Earth is the axis itself: no precession anywhere. Dots mark real installations. A single pendulum sits on one dot and cannot tell the models apart; the argument is the shape of the curve the dots lie on, and it is a sign and a zero crossing, not a small difference in size. The pendulum run at the South Pole in 2001 turned the other way from every northern installation [1]. Geometrically, the daily turning measures the curvature enclosed by the pendulum's path, which is why the result is taught as a theorem about spheres [2][3].
lat.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: pendulums turning the same way in both hemispheres, with no zero at the equator.
ellipse.title: The pendulum's own error, and how to cancel it
ellipse.mini: If the bob traces a thin ellipse, the ellipse precesses by itself, at a rate set by its area, and in the sense the bob circulates. The Earth's precession does not care how the bob was released, so averaging opposite releases removes it.
ellipse.text: A pendulum of length L whose bob traces a thin ellipse, with semi-axes a and b, rather than a straight line. The ellipse precesses on its own, for reasons that have nothing to do with the Earth, at a rate proportional to ab/L², worked out by Airy in 1851. Its sense follows the direction the bob circulates, so starting it the other way reverses it. The Earth's precession does not: at a given latitude it has the same rate and sense every time. So releasing the bob a dozen times with opposite ellipses and averaging separates the two; what survives is the Earth. A modern study measured both effects on one 4.8 m pendulum and found the interplay the formulas predict [1]. The ellipse is greatly exaggerated in the drawing.
ellipse.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: a precession that reverses when the release is reversed, leaving nothing after averaging.
